title: Early Archaic settlement of Trinidad
body: Early Archaic communities settled Trinidad from the nearby South American mainland.

title: Earliest known occupation of Banwari Trace
body: Banwari Trace contains the oldest currently known archaeological evidence of human settlement in the West Indies. It's earliest midden deposits date to approximately 7800–7900 cal BP, or c. 5900 BC.
source: Tankersley et al. (2018), “Geochronology and Paleoenvironmental Framework for the Oldest Archaeological Site…,” Latin American Antiquity 29(4): 681–695. https://doi.org/10.1017/laq.2018.49

title: Early plant cultivation at St. John
body: Starch residues on grindstones show that early communities processed maize, sweet potato, chili pepper, yams and other plants by approximately 7790 cal BP.
source: Pagán-Jiménez, Jaime R., Reniel Rodríguez-Ramos, Basil A. Reid, Martijn van den Bel, and Corinne L. Hofman. 2015. “Early Dispersals of Maize and Other Food Plants into the Southern Caribbean and Northeastern South America.” Quaternary Science Reviews 123: 231–246.

title: Occupation of Ortoire
body: Late Archaic communities occupied the Ortoire shell-midden complex, the type site from which the archaeological name “Ortoiroid” was derived.

title: Saladoid settlement of Trinidad
body: Saladoid communities established settlements in Trinidad and produced distinctive ceramics. The earliest local expression is known as the Cedros complex; it later developed into the more widespread Palo Seco complex.
source: Boomert, Faber-Morse and Rouse (2013), The 1946 and 1953 Yale University Excavations in Trinidad, Yale University Publications in Anthropology 92

title: Emergence of the Erin complex
body: Barrancoid ceramic traditions from the Lower Orinoco became integrated with Trinidad’s existing Late Palo Seco tradition. Both pottery traditions were made and used together, suggesting exchange, coexistence and likely intermarriage.

title: Emergence of the Bontour complex
body: A new local ceramic complex developed through interaction between Trinidad and Arauquinoid communities of the Lower Orinoco. Bontour pottery was generally shell-tempered and minimally decorated.

title: Bontour settlements expand across Trinidad
body: Bontour settlements became widespread along the coast and inland, indicating increasing population density and island-wide exchange.

title: Emergence of the Mayoid tradition
body: The Mayoid ceramic tradition reached Trinidad from the Guiana coastal region several centuries before European contact. It overlapped with the older Bontour complex and featured thin-walled bowls and necked jars with minimal decoration.
source: Boomert, Arie. 2016. The Indigenous Peoples of Trinidad and Tobago: From the First Settlers Until Today

title: Columbus encounters Trinidad
body: During his third voyage, Christopher Columbus sighted Trinidad, named the island “Trinidad,” and recorded houses and people near the southeastern coast.
source: Columbus, Christopher. 1498. “Narrative of the Third Voyage,” in Select Letters of Christopher Columbus, trans. R. H. Major, 1870, pp. 108–174

title: Spanish Crown authorizes Indigenous enslavement
body: A royal order classified Trinidad and several Lesser Antillean islands as “Carib” territories, authorizing Spanish colonists to wage war, capture inhabitants and enslave them. Trinidad subsequently became a target of raids connected to the pearl fisheries around Margarita and Cubagua.
source: “Licencia para hacer guerra a los caribes,” 24 Dec. 1511, Archivo General de Indias, Indiferente General 418, L.3, fol. 91r

title: Antonio Sedeño appointed governor
body: The Spanish Crown appointed Antonio Sedeño captain and governor-general of Trinidad and authorized him to establish a colony. He arrived on 8 November 1530 with two ships and approximately seventy men.
source: Fernández de Oviedo, Historia general y natural de las Indias, vol. II, book 24, chapters 2–4

title: First Battle of Cumucurapo
body: After Sedeño’s forces raided Indigenous food supplies, communities around Cumucurapo resisted the attempted settlement. The Spaniards destroyed the village but lacked provisions and withdrew to Margarita.
source: Aguado, Recopilación historial, part II, book 4

title: Second Battle of Cumucurapo
body: Sedeño returned and constructed a fortified settlement at Cumucurapo. Indigenous forces attacked it; the Spaniards held the position and rebuilt their defenses.
source: Aguado, Recopilación historial, part II, book 4

title: Sedeño abandons Cumucurapo
body: Unable to sustain the colony or retain enough settlers, Sedeño withdrew. Spain did not establish a lasting settlement in Trinidad during this attempt.
source: National Trust of Trinidad and Tobago, “T&T History Timeline”

title: Roume de Saint-Laurent visits Trinidad
body: Grenada planter Philippe-Rose Roume de Saint-Laurent visited Trinidad and assessed its prospects for settlement and plantation development. His reports and lobbying proposed attracting Roman Catholic settlers from other Caribbean colonies, contributing to the policy later formalized in the 1783 Cédula.
source: Roume de Saint-Laurent, “Report to Lord Macartney, Governor of Grenada, of His Visit to Trinidad,” 1777, Colonial Office records, CO 101/20, reproduced as Publication No. 604

title: Cédula of Population issued
body: The Spanish Crown offered land and tax incentives to foreign Roman Catholics who settled in Trinidad. White settlers received approximately 32 acres and additional land for each enslaved person they introduced; free Black and mixed-race household heads received half the allocation offered to white settlers. The policy accelerated migration from the French Caribbean and expanded plantation slavery.
source: Charles III of Spain, Real Cédula para la población y comercio de la isla de Trinidad, 24 November 1783; English translation in Report of the Commissioners of Inquiry into Titles to Lands in Trinidad, 1827, pp. 191–194

title: Chacón begins implementing the Cédula
body: Governor José María Chacón arrived to administer immigration and land grants. He transferred the Cabildo from St Joseph to the growing settlement of Port of Spain.
source: NALIS, “Local Government”

title: Early sugar production expands
body: French planter Picot de Lapeyrouse established an early sugar mill at the Tragarete estate. New estates producing sugar, cotton, coffee and cocoa expanded alongside enslaved African labour.
source: Caribbean Library Journal, vol. 3

title: French Caribbean migration accelerates
body: Revolutionary unrest in the French Caribbean encouraged additional migration to Trinidad. French and French Creole became widely spoken, while plantation agriculture and enslavement expanded.
site: Port of Spain and plantation districts
source: UWI, “Patois History”

title: Small Sephardic Jewish presence
body: A small number of Sephardic Jewish merchants and families arrived from Suriname, Curaçao, Iberian and South American networks. Intermarriage and assimilation prevented the formation of a lasting organized congregation.
source: Joanna Newman, Nearly the New World: The British West Indies and the Flight from Nazism, 1933–1945 (2019); Jewish Telegraphic Agency, “The Jews of Trinidad”

title: San Fernando established as a town
body: Governor Chacón declared San Fernando a town as settlement and plantation agriculture expanded in southern Trinidad.
source: NALIS, “Historical Sketch of San Fernando”

title: French-speaking society under British rule
body: Britain captured Trinidad from Spain. The island entered British rule with a large French-speaking population, approximately 10,000 enslaved people and more than 4,000 free Black and mixed-race inhabitants.
source: Contemporary 1797 census figures summarized in Trinidad historical records

title: British forces capture Trinidad
body: A British expedition under Sir Ralph Abercromby took Trinidad from Spain; Governor José María Chacón surrendered, and Britain installed Thomas Picton as governor.
source: National Trust timeline; contemporary treaty context

title: Treaty of Amiens formalizes British rule
body: Spain ceded Trinidad to Britain in full sovereignty. British rule retained much of the island’s French-speaking population and Spanish legal inheritance.
source: Treaty of Amiens, Article IV

title: First Chinese migrants arrive on the Fortitude
body: The East India Company ship Fortitude arrived with 192 Chinese migrants recruited through Macao, Penang and Canton. This was the first recorded organized Chinese migration to Trinidad.
source: Walton Look Lai, “The Chinese in Trinidad, 1806–1838,” Caribbean Quarterly

title: Colonial government frames Chinese migration as “free cultivators”
body: Governor Thomas Hislop issued a proclamation presenting the newcomers as free agricultural labourers, part of Britain’s effort to develop Trinidad’s plantation economy.
source: Hislop proclamation, 1806, quoted in The Chinese in Trinidad, 1806–1838

title: First migration experiment breaks down
body: The original group faced illness, conflict and plantation conditions; 61 left Trinidad in 1807, and only 22 reportedly remained by 1810. This was not yet a continuous settler community.
source: Walton Look Lai, “The Chinese in Trinidad, 1806–1838,” Caribbean Quarterly

title: Great Fire of Port of Spain
body: A fire destroyed much of Port of Spain. In its aftermath, colonial authorities introduced building regulations and rebuilt major public structures in brick.
source: Parliament of Trinidad and Tobago

title: Britain abolishes the transatlantic slave trade
body: Britain abolished its legal transatlantic slave trade in 1807. British naval patrols thereafter intercepted illegal slave ships, and some liberated Africans were brought to Trinidad.
source: National Trust timeline

title: First documented Portuguese arrivals
body: The Stralhista arrived from Madeira with 28 passengers, marking the earliest documented Madeiran Portuguese arrival in Trinidad.
source: Jo-Anne S. Ferreira, The Portuguese of Trinidad and Tobago; Portuguese community timeline

title: Slavery abolished; apprenticeship ends
body: Enslavement formally ended in British colonies in 1834; Trinidad’s apprenticeship system ended in 1838, completing legal emancipation.
source: British emancipation records / Trinidad historical timeline

title: Indian indentureship begins
body: The Fatel Razack arrived on 30 May with the first group of Indian indentured labourers, beginning a major migration that reshaped Trinidad.
source: National Trust timeline

title: Madeiran Protestant refugees arrive
body: Several ships carried Madeiran Presbyterian refugees expelled amid religious persecution. Many joined Greyfriars Church in Port of Spain; many also left Trinidad for the United States by 1849.
source: Passenger lists and church-history record

title: Madeiran contract labour migration begins
body: The Senator arrived from Madeira with 219 contract labourers. British colonial authorities recruited Madeirans amid labour shortages after emancipation.
source: Ferreira, The Portuguese of Trinidad and Tobago; UWI research on Madeiran migration

title: Portuguese settlers enter small trade
body: Some Madeiran migrants left contract labour for small business—opening dry-goods shops, rum shops and other enterprises. The community built commercial networks in Port of Spain and throughout Trinidad.
source: Ferreira, The Portuguese of Trinidad and Tobago; UWI research on Madeiran migration

title: Chinese indentured immigration resumes
body: Colonial correspondence documents a new introduction of Chinese indentured workers to Trinidad and British Guiana as planters sought labour after the end of apprenticeship in 1838.
source: British Parliamentary Papers, Copies or Extracts of Despatches Relating to Chinese Immigrants…, 1853

title: Larger Chinese immigration programme begins
body: A later and more sustained immigration wave brought Chinese labourers to Trinidad under indenture, contributing to the foundations of the present-day Chinese-Trinidadian community.
source: Walton Look Lai, The Chinese in the West Indies, 1806–1995

title: Portuguese community expands
body: Continued migration and family settlement created communities in Port of Spain, Arima, Arouca, Chaguanas and San Fernando. By the end of the nineteenth century, the Madeiran community numbered roughly 2,000.
site: Port of Spain; San Fernando; Arima
source: Ferreira, The Portuguese of Trinidad and Tobago; UWI research on Madeiran migration

title: Chinese migrants build retail and commercial networks
body: As indentures ended, many Chinese Trinidadians moved into shopkeeping, food retail, trades and small business. Kinship and credit networks supported movement from rural districts into towns.
site: Port of Spain, San Fernando, Arima
source: National Library and Information System Authority, Chinese heritage resources

title: Trinidad and Tobago united administratively
body: Britain united Trinidad and Tobago into a single colony, a political arrangement that continued until independence.
source: West India Committee

title: Chain migration and community continuity
body: Migration continued from Madeira and through other Caribbean territories, while Portuguese Trinidadians expanded into commerce, food production and professional life.
source: Ferreira, The Portuguese of Trinidad and Tobago

title: First documented Syrian and Lebanese settlers
body: Families from Ottoman Greater Syria—the region later divided into Syria, Lebanon and other states—were recorded in Trinidad by 1902. Most early migrants were Arabic-speaking Christians seeking economic opportunity and relief from political and social instability.
site: Marine Square and east Port of Spain
source: NALIS, “Syrian Lebanese”

title: Syrian-Lebanese migration develops
body: Early settlers included George Habib, Amin Abraham, Abdullah Gabriel and Elias Galy. Most initial migrants were men who lived in boarding houses around Marine Square, George, Duke, Duncan and Charlotte Streets.
source: NALIS, “Syrian Lebanese”

title: Peddling and family networks establish the community
body: Many migrants began as travelling peddlers selling cloth and small goods throughout Trinidad. Established merchants supplied newcomers with goods on credit; earnings were used to support relatives and finance further family migration.
source: NALIS, “Syrian Lebanese”; Caribbean Beat, “Feast from the East”

title: Syrian-Lebanese community recorded in the census
body: The 1921 colonial census recorded 108 Trinidad residents whose birthplace was classified as “Arabia,” the administrative category then used for many migrants from Greater Syria.
source: Census of the Colony of Trinidad and Tobago, 1921, cited in da Silva Lopes and Casson, “From Sugar to Shop”

title: Second Syrian-Lebanese migration wave
body: A second migration wave arrived between the world wars, including families from Syria’s Christian Valley and Lebanon. Chain migration reunited families and expanded communities in Port of Spain and San Fernando.
site: Port of Spain and San Fernando
source: NALIS, “Syrian Lebanese”; Besson, “Syrian-Lebanese Community”

title: Legislative Council gains elected members
body: Constitutional reforms expanded elected representation, though British colonial officials retained decisive power.
source: Trinidad and Tobago constitutional history records

title: Jewish refugees begin arriving
body: Small numbers of Jews escaping antisemitism in Central and Eastern Europe began arriving in Trinidad. These arrivals preceded the larger refugee movement following Nazi Germany’s annexation of Austria.
source: UWI, Historical Notes on the Jews in Trinidad, SC42

title: Butler labour uprisings
body: Oilfield and sugar-worker protests became a decisive challenge to colonial labour conditions and helped shape the modern trade-union and nationalist movements.
source: Trinidad and Tobago labour-history records

title: Jewish refugees flee to Trinidad
body: Approximately 500 Jews from Germany, Austria and Czechoslovakia reached Trinidad by the end of 1938. Trinidad became a last-chance refuge because entry initially required a landing deposit rather than a visa.
source: Newman, Nearly the New World; Newman, PhD thesis, University of Southampton, 1998

title: Jewish Religious Society established
body: Refugees established Trinidad’s first organized Jewish congregation, the Jewish Religious Society. Community life later included worship spaces, aid organizations, Hebrew classes, Yiddish theatre and social clubs.
source: Jewish Telegraphic Agency, “The Jews of Trinidad”

title: Trinidad restricts refugee entry
body: As applications from European refugees increased, Trinidad’s colonial government prohibited further refugee immigration from Europe, closing an important escape route shortly before the Holocaust escalated.
source: Newman, Nearly the New World, 2019

title: Jewish community reaches about 600
body: By March 1940, records counted 585 Jewish refugees in Trinidad. The community became informally known as the “Calypso Jews” or “Calypso Shtetl.”
source: Newman, Nearly the New World; Commonwealth Jewish Council

title: Jewish refugees interned as “enemy aliens”
body: British colonial authorities interned refugees holding German and Austrian nationality despite their flight from Nazi persecution. Camps operated at St James and Nelson Island; most refugee internments occurred between May 1940 and December 1941.
site: Camp Rented, St James; Nelson Island
source: Newman, “Internment,” in The Last Goldfish dossier

title: Refugees released under restrictions
body: Remaining Jewish internees were released, but many remained subject to curfews, movement restrictions and police reporting requirements until the war ended.
source: Newman, Nearly the New World; Commonwealth Jewish Council

title: Universal adult suffrage introduced
body: Adults gained the vote without property or income qualifications, expanding political participation before self-government and independence.
source: Trinidad and Tobago constitutional history records

title: Jewish refugees leave or settle permanently
body: Most refugees subsequently emigrated to the United States, Canada, Venezuela or Palestine, while a smaller number remained and contributed to Trinidad’s commercial and cultural life.
source: Newman, Nearly the New World; Jewish Telegraphic Agency

title: Mediterranean Star founded
body: Eight women established the Mediterranean Star, later renamed the Syrian Lebanese Women’s Association of Trinidad and Tobago. It became a centre for charitable work and preserving food, music, dance and other cultural traditions.
source: Syrian Lebanese Women’s Association history; Trinidad and Tobago Newsday

title: PNM wins the general election
body: Eric Williams’s People’s National Movement won office, beginning the final phase of British colonial rule and the drive toward independence.
source: Trinidad and Tobago election history

title: Trinidad and Tobago becomes independent
body: Trinidad and Tobago became an independent state within the Commonwealth, ending British colonial rule.
source: Trinidad and Tobago independence records
